articles.content: Iran says three tankers hit mines, yet oil sits near a three-month low as supply wins ICYMI: China's 90 billion yuan rescue: record state ETF buying struggles to halt AI sell-off CFTC staff let exchanges count bitcoin and ether toward reserves, after a 20% haircut PIMCO: AI debt and refinancing stress are splitting the corporate bond market in two Gold's road back to $5,000: four big banks bet on recovery, but the Fed sets the pace BlackRock says markets overprice Fed hikes, sees two not three as energy shock fades PBOC sets USD/ CNY central rate at 6.7111 (vs. estimate at 6.6757) Singapore sees AI boom carrying 2026, but slower AI investment growth to weigh on 2027 Bank of Korea seen hiking to 3.25% this week, with one final move in early 2027 Analysts cheer Huang's Nvidia return but question the board's sudden U-turn Singapore Q3 GDP jumps 6.1%, growth forecast lifted to around 6% as exports boom NinjaTrader Bid/Ask data change: does it affect your indicators and Tick Replay? Goldman says AI's next test is proving the economics, not the technology Fed's Williams won't rule out back-to-back rate hikes as data drives the path ANZ pulls first RBA rate cut forward to June 2027, sees three cuts by early 2028 Tokyo gets its first look at the Nvidia whiplash as Asia trades the Huang rebound Goldman sees up to $15 trillion for AI infrastructure as spending spreads beyond Nvidia Fed's Williams pins inflation on unusual factors, sees 2027 bringing it lower Nvidia's Huang is back. Monday's rally leaves three big questions unanswered. Jensen Huang is back in charge. Nvidia moves higher. investingLive Americas market news wrap: Nvidia climbs 30% as Jensen Huang returns Summary: The Kospi jumped about 7% and the Nikkei nearly 4% as Huang's return to Nvidia revived the AI trade, led by SK Hynix and Samsung Chinese stocks edged up from a 16-month low after record state ETF buying, while the Hang Seng slipped to its weakest since April 2025 JGBs rallied across the curve, with the 10-year yield down about 8bp to 2.70%, as Japan's flash PMI showed factories strong and services slowing Fed's Williams left back-to-back hikes on the table, while BlackRock argued markets are pricing too many The BOK is seen hiking to 3.25% on Thursday, and ANZ brought its first RBA cut forward to June 2027 Singapore's Q3 GDP grew 6.1%, and its 2026 forecast was raised to around 6% Oil held near a three-month low as supply outweighed Hormuz risk, gold steadied above $3,600 and bitcoin slipped toward $60,000, and dipped under Asian stock markets staged a powerful rebound on Tuesday as Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive revived the AI trade, with South Korea's Kospi jumping about 7% and Japan's Nikkei gaining nearly 4%. Chinese shares lagged despite record state support, while oil hovered near a three-month low and the day's central bank commentary kept the focus on how much further the Fed will tighten. AI rebound lifts Asia The rally followed Wall Street's best session since April 2025, after Nvidia's board unanimously voted to bring Huang back. Korea led the region. The Kospi climbed around 7% to about 5,040, recovering the 5,000 level, and the Kosdaq rose about 5%. Memory chipmakers did the heavy lifting, with SK Hynix up about 8.6% and Samsung Electronics up about 8.2%. The rebound came a day after Seoul said it was ready to activate a market stabilisation fund of about 10.8 trillion won. In Tokyo, which reopened after Monday's holiday, the Nikkei rose about 4% to around 58,670 and the Topix gained about 2.5%. Analysts broadly welcomed Huang's return as removing a major source of uncertainty for the AI sector, although some questioned the credibility of Nvidia's board after its reversal a week after ruling out his comeback. Chinese and Hong Kong shares were more subdued. The Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.5% to around 3,555, rebounding from a 16-month low hit on Monday, and the tech-focused STAR50 rose 2.5%. State-backed funds bought a record 90 billion yuan of ETFs on Friday and exchanges eased margin rules over the weekend. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 0.5% to its weakest since April 2025, with an AI index giving up an early 6% gain. One fund manager said Huang's return would help Chinese firms in Nvidia's supply chain but would not ease US chip controls on China. Japan: bonds and stocks rally together Japanese government bonds rallied across the curve after the three-day weekend, with gains holding even as equities surged. The 2-year yield fell about 5 basis points to around 1.78% and the 10-year about 8 basis points to around 2.70%. The flash November PMI showed Japan's economy splitting in two, with manufacturing rising to 53.7 on the strongest export orders since 2018 while services growth slowed to 50.5. Business optimism fell to its joint-lowest since 2020, though S&P Global said stubborn price pressures continue to back expectations of a Bank of Japan hike in December. USD/JPY held near 159. Fed: hawks and doubters New York Fed President John Williams said inflation remains too high and that he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if needed, while describing recent price pressures as driven by unusual factors and calling 2027 a year of lower inflation. He said tech-sector volatility had not upended his positive outlook. BlackRock took the other side of the debate, arguing markets are pricing too many hikes. It expects a December move and one more in the first half of 2027, as the energy shock's boost to inflation reverses. US 10-year Treasury yields held around 4.90%, and US stock index futures edged higher. Asia-Pacific central banks A Reuters poll showed 32 of 34 economists expect the Bank of Korea to raise its base rate to 3.25% on Thursday, with a final hike to 3.50% seen by the end of the first quarter of 2027. ANZ brought forward its forecast for the first Reserve Bank of Australia rate cut to June 2027 from November, citing a weakening labour market, and now sees three cuts taking the cash rate to 4.10% by February 2028. AUD/USD was flat around 0.6630. Singapore's economy grew 6.1% in the third quarter from a year earlier, well above the 5.4% advance estimate, and the government raised its 2026 growth forecast to around 6% on AI-related export demand. It expects growth to slow to 2.5% to 4.5% in 2027 as the pace of new AI investment moderates. AI's bigger picture Goldman Sachs estimated that $10 trillion to $15 trillion could flow into AI infrastructure over the next six years, with spending increasingly reaching memory, packaging and power beyond Nvidia, and said the AI debate is shifting from proving the technology to proving the economics. PIMCO said heavy AI borrowing by the largest tech companies has squeezed the gap between top-rated and lower-rated investment grade bonds to a record low, while the weakest junk-rated borrowers face recession-like refinancing stress. Oil, gold and crypto Oil held near a three-month low, with WTI just under $80 a barrel, as rising supply outweighed renewed risk in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran said three tankers hit mines. Deutsche Bank estimated an oversupply of 1.7 million barrels a day in October. Gold steadied above $3,600 an ounce after last week's 9% slide, as Goldman Sachs, UBS, Bank of America and Societe Generale all forecast a recovery in 2027 but differed on its timing. Silver fell more than 1% to around $42.70. Bitcoin slipped about 1.7% to around $60,300, while US derivatives regulators said exchanges and clearinghouses may count discounted bitcoin, ether and payment stablecoins toward their financial reserves. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Vitamin D levels, fatigue self-efficacy, and pain severity among patients with multiple sclerosis: A cross-sectional study in Saudi Arabia
articles.desc: Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease in which fatigue and pain are common and disabling symptoms. Vitamin D exerts pleiotropic immunomodulatory and neuroprotective effects that are biologically relevant to MS, yet its association with fatigue self-efficacy and pain
articles.content: Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic immune-mediated disease in which fatigue and pain are common and disabling symptoms. Vitamin D exerts pleiotropic immunomodulatory and neuroprotective effects that are biologically relevant to MS, yet its association with fatigue self-efficacy and pain severity remains uncertain and has rarely been examined in Middle Eastern populations. This study examined the linear and non-linear associations between serum vitamin D, fatigue self-efficacy, and pain outcomes among patients with MS attending neurology services in the Qassim region of Saudi Arabia. Methods An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 246 patients with MS recruited by convenience sampling from neurology inpatient and outpatient services in the Qassim region between July and December 2025. All participants had a physician-established diagnosis of MS documented in the medical record. Serum vitamin D values were abstracted from medical records. Fatigue self-efficacy was assessed with the Fatigue Self-Efficacy Scale, and pain was assessed with the Arabic Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire. Unadjusted comparisons were examined using t-tests, analysis of variance, and Pearson chi-square or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) with penalized spline smoothers were then used to examine non-linear partial effects of vitamin D on fatigue self-efficacy and total pain burden after adjustment for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and MS-related work interference. Sensitivity analyses restricted to participants whose most recent serum vitamin D measurement fell within the preceding five months were also performed. Predictor hierarchy was examined using multivariable models with standardized coefficients. Results Participants had a mean age of 32.6 ± 9.9 years, 64.2% were women, and the mean serum vitamin D was 22.8 ± 11.0 ng/mL; 178 of 242 participants (73.6%) were below the sufficiency threshold used in the source database. In unadjusted analyses, the vitamin D category was associated with age, MS-related work impact, time since the last relapse, and present pain intensity. GAMs identified a significant non-linear partial association of vitamin D with fatigue self-efficacy (effective degrees of freedom [EDoF] = 12.6, p < 0.001); the corresponding smooth term for total pain burden was also significant (EDoF = 12.6, p < 0.001), although this association was attenuated in sensitivity analyses restricted to recent vitamin D measurements and should be regarded as provisional. In the standardized predictor models, MS-related work interference showed the largest observed adjusted association with lower fatigue self-efficacy (B = −4.16, β = −0.22, p < 0.001), whereas BMI showed the largest observed adjusted association with total pain burden (B = −0.16, β = −0.21, p = 0.001). Conclusions Vitamin D status was associated with MS symptom burden through complex non-linear patterns rather than simple linear associations. In this cohort, however, MS-related work interference and BMI showed stronger observed adjusted associations with fatigue self-efficacy and pain burden, respectively, than vitamin D concentration alone. These are cross-sectional associations and do not establish causal or temporal relationships. Comprehensive MS care should therefore integrate metabolic assessment with functional and psychosocial support.

articles.title: vCISO Lite Launches vCISO Lite for Consultants: The Services Do the Work, the Consultant Makes the Call
articles.desc: Independent vCISOs and fractional CISOs run six engagements on vCISO Lite’s own services and deliver outcomes their clients can verify
articles.content: vCISO Lite Launches vCISO Lite for Consultants: The Services Do the Work, the Consultant Makes the Call There were 2,101 press releases posted in the last 24 hours and 505,936 in the last 365 days. vCISO Lite Launches vCISO Lite for Consultants: The Services Do the Work, the Consultant Makes the Call Practioner's prioritized view of their full slate of clients and engagements [Fictional] Kestrel Bio's SOC2 Readiness Assessment mid engagement [Fictional] Vendor Risk Assessment for Reliance Labs with potential financial losses due to findings Independent vCISOs and fractional CISOs run six engagements on vCISO Lite’s own services and deliver outcomes their clients can verify We’re offering the underlying vCISO Lite services to consultants to make it easier to complete an engagement. This will lead to greater client retention, practice growth & increased profitability.” ATLANTA, GA, UNITED STATES, November 23, 2026 / today launched vCISO Lite for Consultants for independent vCISOs, fractional CISOs and small practices. Inside each engagement, the vCISO Lite service that does the work, whether red team testing, compliance grading, vendor analysis, risk quantification or policy drafting, runs it against the client's own systems. The consultant sees what the service found, the evidence behind it, the client policy it breaks and the date it puts at risk, then makes the call in place. The deliverable is the service's own report, and anyone the client shares it with can check where every finding came from. Charter practitioners can start today at advisory.vcisolite.com. For most independent practitioners, the hours go to assembly rather than judgment. Evidence is requested by email and pasted into spreadsheets. Findings are mapped to policy by hand. Reports are rebuilt from the last one. The consultant's expertise gets maybe a third of the engagement. "We're taking the underlying services which enable vCISO Lite and providing them programmatically for consultants to make it easier, faster and more consistent to complete an engagement," said Yolonda Smith, founder of vCISO Lite. "Our expectation is that this will lead to greater client retention, practice growth and increased profitability per consultant." - Red team. Tests run against targets the client has verified, in staging or production. Each failure arrives with its request and response, the client policy clause it breaks, with the MITRE ATT&CK technique where no clause applies, and the hosts it affects. The retest is included. - Audit readiness. Each requirement of SOC 2, ISO 27001, CMMC, PCI DSS, HIPAA, NIST CSF, ISO42001 and dozens of others are graded from evidence read directly from the client's systems. The consultant confirms each grade, accepts it with noted gaps, or attests. An auditor can be invited as a read-only guest. - Vendor review. Vendor answers are analyzed against the client's own policies, and violations are cited by clause. The consultant records a go, conditional or no-go decision for each vendor. - Risk assessment. The client's loss scenarios are priced and compared with a tolerance computed from its business. The consultant records whether each risk is mitigated, accepted, transferred or avoided. - Policy Generation. Policies are drafted clause by clause. Missing facts stay visible instead of being made up, and the client approves each revision. - Questionnaire response. A customer's security questionnaire is drafted from the client's evidence and written back into the customer's own workbook. Every record shows where it came from: collected by a service, provided by the client, provided by the consultant, or the consultant's own judgment. Records are sealed when they are written. While the work is underway, the client's portal shows what they granted and every read a service made under it. After delivery, an auditor, board or acquirer can verify the report without an account and without the consultant. Prices are published and there is no sales call. Solo

articles.title: Su-30MKI's High-Angle Control Edge and Localized Maintenance Sustain
articles.desc: The Su-30MKI fighter retains a measurable edge in aerodynamic control over the F-22 Raptor during high-angle-of-attack maneuvers, according to pilot data from Sukhoi's chief test pilot, Sergey Bogdan. In an interview with the Zvezda channel's Military Inspection, Bogdan compared the flight envelopes
articles.content: The Su-30MKI fighter retains a measurable edge in aerodynamic control over the F-22 Raptor during high-angle-of-attack maneuvers, according to pilot data from Sukhoi's chief test pilot, Sergey Bogdan. In an interview with the Zvezda channel's Military Inspection, Bogdan compared the flight envelopes of the two aircraft, noting that the Su-30MKI executes complex flight regimes with greater stability than the F-22, even when the latter is performing at maximum agility. For the defense manufacturing sector, this distinction matters because sustained control at high angles of attack determines survivability in close-range combat, a metric that directly influences export contract renewals. Production System: From Flight Test to Export Hub The operational longevity of the Su-30 family is driven by a shift in the production and support model. Rather than relying solely on direct supply of new airframes from Russian manufacturers, the supply chain is expanding through localized maintenance and upgrade centers. This approach reduces bottlenecks associated with international component logistics and extends the usable service life of existing airframes. India has emerged as the central node in this ecosystem. As the primary operator of the Su-30MKI, the country is not only maintaining its fleet but also developing indigenous upgrade capabilities. A key component of this strategy is the Virupaksha radar, a passive electronically scanned array system being developed domestically. The integration of such systems into the Su-30 frame allows for continued technological relevance without requiring a full airframe replacement.

articles.title: North Country farmers getting $2.17M in tariff relief
articles.desc: Millions of dollars in tariff relief are going to 177 farmers in the North Country.
articles.content: North Country farmers getting $2.17M in tariff relief ALBANY, New York (WWNY) - Millions of dollars in tariff relief are going to 177 farmers in the North Country. Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Monday that $23 million is on its way to farmers across New York. She said the money will help them offset rising costs and market losses caused by federal tariffs. In the North Country, 177 farmers are getting $2.17 million. Payments range from $1,000 to $25,000. “President Trump started this trade war and New York’s farmers shouldn’t have to pay the price,” Hochul said. “With reckless tariffs hurting the farmers who feed our families, New York is stepping up to provide direct relief through my Agricultural Resiliency Against Tariffs Program. When Washington turns its back on our producers and growers here in New York, we’re working to ensure that New York’s family farms have a future, not just a proud history.” “The detrimental effect of tariffs on certain agricultural commodities is yet another hit to our farmers’ bottom line,” New York Farm Bureau President David Fisher said. ”Farmers are already facing challenging market conditions, weather uncertainties, and the persistently high cost of diesel fuel. The governor’s tariff relief program helps offset these factors. We appreciate the much-needed boost.” “Costs continue to rise across the board, especially labor, utilities, and material inputs – costs that cannot be simply passed on to consumers by dairy farmers since we do not set the price of our milk, said Northeast Dairy Producers Association Chair and Dairy Farmer AJ Wormuth. On our farm, diesel costs alone have doubled in the past six months. As we navigate economic uncertainty and an unpredictable global marketplace, we look forward to continuing to work with the Governor and Legislature and encourage family farms across the state to apply for support through this program. Thank you, Gov. Hochul, for listening to the challenges our farms face, recognizing the opportunities ahead for the dairy industry, and taking steps to strengthen local food security.” Another $7 million in relief remains. Farmers can apply for the second round of funding on Dec. 3. The money is for those who were unable to meet the application timeline of the first round, which launched this summer during the peak of the agricultural season. Copyright 2026 WWNY. articles.title: Blood test may detect CTE in living people’s brains
articles.desc: New findings offer the best hope yet that doctors will one day be able to diagnose the brain disease CTE in the living.
articles.content: Blood test may detect CTE in living people's brains - Futurity You are free to share this article under the Attribution 4.0 International license. A new study identifies a blood test that may detect the brain disease CTE in life. As a quarterback for 18 seasons in the National Football League, Matt Hasselbeck carved out a successful career making crucial decisions when games were on the line. But in 2020, five years removed from his retirement from football, Hasselbeck made perhaps his most consequential decision: The three-time All-Pro selection pledged to donate his brain after his death to Boston University research on chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). A degenerative brain disease connected to repeated hits to the head, particularly in former contact sports athletes, CTE can currently only be detected and diagnosed accurately through autopsy. Hasselbeck is among hundreds of former football players hoping to change that—and a new study suggests their efforts might be starting to pay off, with BU researchers unveiling a potential new CTE blood test. Since making his initial donation commitment, Hasselbeck has also submitted to testing in life. Earlier this year, the former quarterback became an ambassador for the BU-led DIAGNOSE CTE Research Project, which recruits men aged over 50 who played college or professional tackle football for thorough medical and neurological exams. Its goal is not just to diagnose CTE in the living, but to also inform the development of potential new treatments. By signing up to BU research, Hasselbeck is following in the footsteps of his father and former New England Patriot Don Hasselbeck, who made the same commitment before passing away in 2025. “My dad led the way. He pledged his brain, so I looked into it… I wanted to know, what are we saying yes to here?” Hasselbeck says. “I was committed to pledging my brain to somebody upon my death, but I needed someone I could trust, because I only have one brain to give.” Journal of the American Medical Association , demonstrates how important the involvement of former players is to CTE research. The findings offer the best hope yet that doctors will one day be able to diagnose the disease in the living. In a study examining a sample of 21 former football players who had their blood drawn in life and donated their brains to the CTE Center upon their death, a research team led by BU and Banner Health has, for the first time, discovered a way to accurately detect the presence of CTE neuropathology using only a blood test. Michael Alosco, a CTE Center codirector of clinical research who led the study and is its corresponding author, calls the initial findings “a game changer.” “I think this finding will significantly change the landscape for clinical research in CTE moving forward,” he says. “If our finding is validated, having a biomarker that can accurately detect CTE will open the door to diagnosis when people are still living and to an entirely new phase of research, including clinical trials where we can start to focus on treatment.” Of the 21 participants researchers studied, 18 had CTE at autopsy and three did not. Of those with CTE, 16 had high stage and two had low stage; five also had Alzheimer’s disease. The researchers examined participants’ blood for a protein called endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau (eMTBR-tau), a marker of a tangle of misfolded proteins in the brain that also are known to form in Alzheimer’s disease. Researchers observed that blood plasma eMTBR-tau concentrations were significantly higher in participants with high-stage CTE than in those with low-stage or no CTE. Researchers also evaluated a blood marker known to be specific to Alzheimer’s disease changes, called p-tau217. It was only elevated in those who had Alzheimer’s disease. Alosco says this suggests the combination of eMTBR-tau and p-tau217 might be optimal for detecting CTE during life and differentiating from Alzheimer’s disease. “I was shocke

articles.title: Former London fire captain identified in 1968 killing of Jacqueline Dunleavy
articles.desc: London police say a historical homicide investigation has been solved through the use of modern DNA technology and investigative techniques.
articles.content: Jacqueline 'Jackie' Dunleavy: London police solve historical homicide Former London fire captain identified in 1968 killing of Jacqueline Dunleavy Nearly 59 years after the killing of 16-year-old Jacqueline “Jackie” Dunleavy, police in London, Ont., say they have identified the man responsible for her death through new DNA testing and forensic investigative genetic genealogy. The London Police Service announced Monday that investigators have identified Michael Joseph Moore, a former London firefighter who retired as a captain, as the person responsible for Dunleavy’s murder. Police say Moore, who was 25 at the time of the murder, died on March 3, 2018, before he was identified through the investigation. As a result, no criminal charges can be laid. Dunleavy, a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School, was working at Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street near Wharncliffe Road on Jan. 9, 1968. Police say she finished her shift at approximately 6:30 p.m. and was last seen leaving the store on foot. At about 8 p.m., three youths found Dunleavy on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now the site of Matthews Hall on Oxford Street. Emergency responders attended the scene, and she was pronounced dead. GALLERY: Jackie Dunleavy cold case photos Investigators determined Dunleavy had been murdered. While she suffered a head injury, police say the cause of death was strangulation. The case remained unsolved for decades despite an extensive investigation that included witness interviews, the pursuit of numerous leads and the collection and preservation of forensic evidence. “For nearly six decades, Jackie’s family has lived with a loss that no passage of time could ever erase, and with unanswered questions about who was responsible for her death,” Thai Truong, London’s police chief, said during a press conference Monday. “A daughter, a sister, a friend and a young girl who had her entire life ahead of her. Jackie was also the daughter of a London police officer. As chief of police, I recognize the particular significance of that connection to our profession.” According to police, the case was reviewed repeatedly over the years, including through Project Angel, a joint initiative involving the London Police Service and the Ontario Provincial Police between 1997 and 2001. More recently, members of the Major Crime Section conducted a comprehensive review of the investigation, re-examining historical evidence and taking advantage of advances in forensic science. Police say additional DNA testing was conducted on preserved evidence. Investigators worked with forensic laboratory Othram, the Toronto Police Service, the Ontario Provincial Police and the Centre of Forensic Sciences to identify distant genetic relatives linked to an unknown DNA profile and narrow the investigation to a suspect. According to police, investigators conducted further interviews, gathered additional evidence and obtained DNA samples for comparison. Based on the evidence collected, police say they determined the threshold for criminal charges had been met had Moore still been alive. According to police, Michael Joseph Moore was born in Ireland in 1942 and immigrated to Canada in January 1967. At the time of Dunleavy’s murder, police said Moore was living in an apartment on Sprinbank Drive. He had been living in the city for less than a year when Dunleavy was killed. He was described as being about 6′ tall, had dark hair, was typically clean shaven and spoke with an Irish accent and it’s believed the vehicle he drove was a 1964 Ford Galaxy 500, four-door sedan. Det. Mike Budzyn with London police said, “Based on the evidence obtained through this investigation, we are confident that the evidentiary threshold to support criminal charges was met. Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged with Jackie’s murder.” At the time of the murder in January 1968, police said Moore was not a firefighter, but that he joined after and served for appr
